title: Sandbox: a pair with a given sum
lead: A sandbox page, AI-written and not part of the book. It tries one lesson shape on one problem: the obvious way, what the obvious way wastes, the fast way, the insight in one sentence, and a check.
notes: A trial page: nothing here is the book's.

exercises.prompt: The array is sorted and $\mathit{nums}[i] + \mathit{nums}[j]$ is larger than the target. Which pairs are ruled out without being added up?

options: Every pair that uses either of them
None: each pair has to be added up
answer.solution: $\mathit{nums}[i]$ is the smallest number still in play, so every other partner for $\mathit{nums}[j]$ makes a sum at least as large, which is still too big. Pairs with $\mathit{nums}[i]$ and a smaller partner than $\mathit{nums}[j]$ are smaller, so one of them may be the target.

exercises.prompt: The same code is run on an array that is not sorted. What goes wrong?

options: It can answer that there is no pair when there is one
It can return a pair that does not add up to the target
It runs for about $n^2$ steps instead of about $n$
Nothing: sorting only makes it faster
answer.solution: A pair it returns was added up and compared, so it is always right, and each step still moves one pointer, so it still stops within $n - 1$ sums. What fails is the ruling out: without sorted order, the other sums in a row are not all smaller, so a row thrown out unseen may hold the answer.

exercises.prompt: Which of these problems gives way to the same insight, that one comparison on a sorted array rules out a whole row or column of pairs?

options: Count the pairs in a sorted array whose sum is at most a target
Find the most frequent value in an array
Find the longest run of equal values in an array
answer.solution: If $\mathit{nums}[i] + \mathit{nums}[j]$ is at most the target, so is $\mathit{nums}[i]$ with every partner between them: $j - i$ pairs are counted at once and $i$ moves right. If it is larger, every pair with $\mathit{nums}[j]$ is too big and $j$ moves left. The other three need no pairs at all.
